(http://lists.sourceforge.net/lists/listinfo/kvm-devel)
The following patchset adds a driver for Intel's hardware virtualization
extensions to the x86 architecture.  The driver adds a character device
(/dev/kvm) that exposes the virtualization capabilities to userspace.  Using
this driver
column2: a process can run a virtual machine (a ""guest"") in a fully

column1: virtualized PC containing its own virtual hard disks
display.
Using this driver
column2: one can start multiple virtual machines on a host.

column1: Each virtual machine is a process on the host; a virtual cpu is a thread in
that process.  kill(1)
column3: top(1) work as expected.  In effect

column1: driver adds a third execution mode to the existing two: we now have kernel
mode
column3: and guest mode.  Guest mode has its own address space mapping

column1: guest physical memory (which is accessible to user mode by mmap()ing
/dev/kvm).  Guest mode has no access to any I/O devices; any such access is
intercepted and directed to user mode for emulation.
The driver supports i386 and x86_64 hosts and guests.  All combinations are
allowed except x86_64 guest on i386 host.  For i386 guests and hosts
and non-pae paging modes are supported.
SMP hosts and UP guests are supported.  At the moment only Intel
hardware is supported
column2: but AMD virtualization support is being worked on.

column1: Performance currently is non-stellar due to the naive implementation of the
mmu virtualization
column2: which throws away most of the shadow page table entries

column1: every context switch.  We plan to address this in two ways:
- cache shadow page tables across tlb flushes
- wait until AMD and Intel release processors with nested page tables
Currently a virtual desktop is responsive but consumes a lot of CPU.  Under
Windows I tried playing pinball and watching a few flash movies; with a recent
CPU one can hardly feel the virtualization.  Linux/X is slower
to X being in a separate process.
In addition to the driver
column2: you need a slightly modified qemu to provide I/O

column1: device emulation and the BIOS.
Caveats (akpm: might no longer be true):
- The Windows install currently bluescreens due to a problem with the
virtual APIC.  We are working on a fix.  A temporary workaround is to
use an existing image or install through qemu
- Windows 64-bit does not work.  That's also true for qemu
probably a problem with the device model.
